title: Copies Created by Advanced Indexing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of copies created by advanced indexing and name one situation where it is useful.
Apply integer-array indexing to a small NumPy example and inspect the resulting values, shape, or dtype.
Identify one important limitation, boundary case, or validation check for copies created by advanced indexing.

content.intro: This lesson develops topic 172 of the supplied curriculum: **Copies Created by Advanced Indexing**. The main starting point is **Integer-array indexing**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Views and references can share memory, while copies own separate data. Awareness of this difference prevents accidental mutation and helps explain memory/performance trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Copies Created by Advanced Indexing** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Integer-array indexing** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
selected = a[[1, 3]]
selected[0] = 99
print(a.tolist(), selected.tolist())
content_blocks.expected_output:
Observed output in the available validation environment (Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5):
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4] [99, 3]

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a slice owns independent memory
common_mistakes.why: Basic slicing commonly creates a view.
Short timings vary due to startup, cache, and system noise.
